priorInvolvementDisclosure: I authored the frozen Claude v18 REJECT (92b01a7a) whose CLAUDE-HEA18-S1 is one of the three repairs v19 claims. v18 was the first round in six where my verdict matched Codex's, and it came from the method change I made after two consecutive wrong ACCEPTs: enumerate each governing rule's branches and construct my own probes for permissive outcomes rather than replaying Codex's published ones. One matching round is not a track record, and the failure it corrected was invisible to me for five rounds, so I did not treat it as license to relax. Two specific risks were live here. First, v19 answers a finding of mine, which is the configuration in which I have most often been too generous. Second, Codex's HAE18-CX-02 introduced severity into the coverage tuple and forbade a frozen BLOCKER or SHOULD-FIX from being registered ADVISORY-NON-BLOCKING; that laundering hole sat in machinery both of us had worked on for nine rounds without either of us attacking it, which is direct evidence that a branch enumeration I believe complete has repeatedly not been. I therefore probed the severity dimension as my primary target, including whether the new tuple is satisfiable at all given that register entries historically carried no severity field on blocking findings. It is: the register has been backfilled. The third risk, that two earlier wrong ACCEPTs create pressure to reject in compensation, is the one I weighed hardest against the single candidate finding I developed, and I record below why I did not escalate it.

advisories.title: The disposition vocabulary is undefined, and dispositionCheck now makes disposition a pure function of frozen severity, leaving no representable state for a partially repaired blocking finding
advisories.observation: dispositionCheck reads 'a frozen BLOCKER or SHOULD-FIX MUST have register disposition REPAIRED and MUST NOT have ADVISORY-NON-BLOCKING; a frozen ADVISORY MUST have ADVISORY-NON-BLOCKING.' Disposition is therefore derivable from severity and carries no independent information, and fromVnCheck then requires a repair-array entry for every one of them. Neither REPAIRED nor ADVISORY-NON-BLOCKING is defined anywhere in the artifact; there is no disposition vocabulary key and no sentence stating what either value asserts. The case this reaches is real rather than hypothetical: my own frozen v18 verdict records HAE17-CX-01 as PARTIALLY REPAIRED, and v19's register, which pins that same verdict file, records it REPAIRED with an at-string describing v18's repair. The convention that makes this sound, that a residual is re-raised under a fresh finding id in the current round rather than leaving the old id open, is one the lineage follows consistently but states nowhere; the words partial, unrepaired, outstanding and carried-forward do not occur in the subject.
advisories.whyNotShouldFix: No disposition is misclassified today. I checked every register finding from v8 onward against both its frozen severity and what actually happened: 31 REPAIRED and the rest ADVISORY-NON-BLOCKING, zero dispositionCheck violations, and each REPAIRED at-string accurately describes the edit that closed that id. HAE17-CX-01's entry is defensible on the reading that REPAIRED closes the id while the residual travels under a new id, which is exactly what happened when I raised CLAUDE-HEA18-S1, and I verified the same pattern at v11 to v13. The rigidity is also the point of Codex's repair, since the degree of freedom that dispositionCheck removes is the one HAE18-CX-02 showed could launder a blocker into a non-blocking disposition. Escalating an undefined vocabulary when the mechanical behaviour is fully determined and every instance is correct would be the over-correction I flagged as a risk before starting.
advisories.suggestedDisposition: Optional. Define the two disposition values, and state the residual convention in terms, for example that a finding whose requiredRepair is only partly delivered is recorded REPAIRED for that id only when the residual is re-raised under a new id in the current round. A future round may also want a representable state for a blocking finding a successor does not close.

advisories.observation: FC-SUBTYPE-CLASS still exercises no CA-3 row despite CA-3 carrying the largest subtype domain including the deferred KEYCHAIN; destinations.actionSubtype still mixes record and serialized class vocabulary in its requiredness clause before restating it serialized; coveredActs still keys the host classes as CA-1-host-head and CA-4-host against the record vocabulary. I have declined to escalate at v13, v15, v16, v17 and v18 and nothing in v19 alters their consequence.

measurements.severityTupleDetail: This was my primary probe, because laneCheck now compares (id, severity) sets and pairCheck compares (lane, id, severity) triples, while register entries historically carried a severity field only on advisories. Had the backfill been skipped, every blocking finding would compare as (id, None) against (id, SHOULD-FIX) and the artifact would violate its own GOVERNING rule on its own data. The backfill was done: implementing laneCheck and the extractor exactly as written across all fourteen lanes for v8 through v18 gives zero refusals, zero set mismatches, and 64 (lane, id, severity) triples equal in both directions.
measurements.claudeHea18S1Detail: keyTypeTotality now reads 'Every present severity key MUST be an array of objects or a nonnegative integer. Any other shape REFUSES, whether or not a sibling key produced ids', which answers both halves of my finding including the inconsistency I demonstrated where the guard fired only when no sibling produced an id. Re-running my v18 probe, blockers=[{id:X}] with shouldFix={'count':2}, now refuses.
measurements.hae18Cx01Detail: schemasMutuallyExclusive is asserted and enforced: the combined branch requires every present severity member to be a nonnegative integer and refuses an array or any other type, and the severity branch requires findings to be absent. Both of Codex's erasure probes now refuse, the empty variant with findings=[] beside blockers=[{B}] and the nonempty variant with findings=[{A}] beside blockers=[{B}]. A negative integer on a skipped key also refuses, which Codex separately named.
measurements.hae18Cx02Detail: The extractor now retains source severity, from findings[].severity in the combined branch and from the array key in the severity branch, with an item severity that disagrees with its key refusing. perSeverityCount compares each present integer against the count of extracted pairs of that severity rather than a grand total, so Codex's laundering probe with one BLOCKER and one SHOULD-FIX against blockers=0 and shouldFix=2 now refuses on the blocker category. Register coverage is the (lane, id, severity) triple, and dispositionCheck forbids a frozen BLOCKER or SHOULD-FIX from carrying ADVISORY-NON-BLOCKING, which closes the disposition-laundering path Codex demonstrated. I checked that path directly: zero violations across all rounds.
measurements.generativeProbingDetail: Twelve probes were run against the extractor implemented exactly as written, eight of them constructed by me rather than replayed from Codex. Refusing correctly: both Codex erasure probes; the negative skipped integer; the severity-laundering count probe; my own v18 malformed-key case; an item with an absent severity; a duplicate id within a lane; an item severity disagreeing with its array key; findings present as a string; and an empty combined extraction against a positive count. Extracting correctly: a combined file with no integer counts at all, where findings[] is the sole source of truth and absent integers are explicitly not checked; and an all-zero-count file with no arrays, which proves zero findings. No probe produced a silent drop.
measurements.claudeHea18A1Detail: My v18 advisory on the combined cross-check ambiguity is resolved rather than merely registered. perSeverityCount now states 'absent integers are not treated as 0 and are not checked', which removes the strict reading under which a conforming combined file carrying no integer counts would have refused. My probe of that case now extracts normally.

verdictBasis: The dispatch permits ACCEPT only at 0 blockers and 0 SHOULD-FIX. This review returns 0 blockers and 0 SHOULD-FIX, so the verdict is ACCEPT. All three claimed repairs verify by execution rather than by reading. My primary probe was the one that could have broken the artifact on its own data: laneCheck now compares (id, severity) and pairCheck compares (lane, id, severity), while register entries historically carried severity only on advisories, so a skipped backfill would have put v19 in violation of its own GOVERNING rule. The backfill was done and 64 triples reconcile in both directions across fourteen lanes. Codex's two erasure probes, his severity-laundering count probe and his disposition-laundering path all now refuse, and my own v18 malformed-key case refuses under the new keyTypeTotality clause. I ran twelve probes in total, eight of my own construction, and none produced a silent drop; the two that extract do so correctly. My v18 advisory on the cross-check ambiguity was adopted outright. Custody is clean on every pin, all 58 recorded inputs reproduce, the 31 repair-array entries correspond exactly to the 31 REPAIRED ids with no advisory leakage, and no prior repair regressed. One candidate defect was developed and is recorded as an advisory rather than suppressed: dispositionCheck makes disposition a pure function of severity with no representable state for a partially repaired blocking finding, and my own frozen v18 verdict calls HAE17-CX-01 PARTIALLY REPAIRED where the register says REPAIRED. I did not escalate it because no disposition is materially misclassified, the residual convention that makes each instance sound is followed consistently, and rejecting on an undefined vocabulary with fully determined and correct behaviour would be compensating for my two earlier wrong ACCEPTs rather than reviewing this artifact.
